CHAPTER 24 - GENETICS AND SOCIETY

Introduction

The science of genetics does not stay inside the laboratory. Once we understand how genes are inherited, how they can go wrong, and how they can be read and even manipulated, that knowledge touches medicine, agriculture, law and everyday human choices. This chapter looks at genetics AS IT MEETS SOCIETY: the inherited disorders that affect human families, the tools of genetic counselling and prenatal diagnosis, the great effort of the Human Genome Project to read our entire genetic instruction book, the technique of DNA fingerprinting that identifies individuals, the breeding of better crops and livestock, and the ethical questions that all of this raises.

24.1 APPLICATIONS OF GENETICS IN SOCIETY

Genetics has given society enormous power. In MEDICINE it explains inherited disease, allows carriers to be identified, and underlies gene therapy and personalised treatment. In AGRICULTURE selective breeding and modern biotechnology have produced high-yielding, disease-resistant and nutritious crops that feed billions. In LAW AND FORENSICS DNA fingerprinting settles questions of identity, paternity and crime. Along with this power come responsibilities, because decisions about genes affect real people, communities and future generations.

24.2 HUMAN GENETIC DISORDERS

A GENETIC DISORDER is a disease caused by an abnormality in an individual's genome. Some are caused by a change (mutation) in a single gene - these are MENDELIAN disorders, inherited in the patterns Mendel described. Others are caused by a change in the number or structure of whole chromosomes - these are CHROMOSOMAL disorders.

(a) MENDELIAN (SINGLE-GENE) DISORDERS

These arise from mutation in a single gene and are passed on according to the rules of dominance and recessiveness, and of autosomal or sex-linked inheritance. Common examples studied in this course are:

SICKLE-CELL ANAEMIA is an autosomal RECESSIVE disorder. A single base change in the gene for the beta-globin chain of haemoglobin substitutes the amino acid valine for glutamic acid. The abnormal haemoglobin (HbS) makes red blood cells collapse into a rigid sickle shape when oxygen is low. These cells block small blood vessels and are destroyed quickly, causing anaemia and pain. A person with two mutant alleles (HbS HbS) is affected; a person with one mutant and one normal allele (HbA HbS) is a healthy CARRIER whose blood shows sickle-cell trait. Interestingly, carriers are partly protected against malaria, which is why the allele persists in malaria-prone regions.

THALASSAEMIA is also an autosomal RECESSIVE blood disorder, but here the problem is REDUCED or ABSENT synthesis of one of the globin chains (alpha or beta), so too little normal haemoglobin is made. Patients suffer chronic anaemia and often need repeated blood transfusions. Unlike sickle-cell anaemia, which is a qualitative defect (wrong haemoglobin), thalassaemia is a quantitative defect (too little haemoglobin).

PHENYLKETONURIA (PKU) is an autosomal RECESSIVE inborn error of metabolism. The affected person lacks the enzyme that converts the amino acid phenylalanine to tyrosine. Phenylalanine and its by-products build up, damaging the developing brain and causing mental retardation. Detected early by newborn screening, PKU can be managed with a phenylalanine-restricted diet.

HAEMOPHILIA is a SEX-LINKED (X-linked) RECESSIVE disorder in which the blood does not clot properly because a clotting factor is missing. Because the gene lies on the X chromosome, it appears far more often in males (who have only one X). A famous pedigree is that of Queen Victoria's descendants, through whom haemophilia spread into several European royal families. Affected males inherit the defective X from carrier mothers.

COLOUR BLINDNESS (red-green) is another X-LINKED RECESSIVE trait. The affected person cannot distinguish red from green because of a defect in the cone-cell pigments. Like haemophilia it is much commoner in males, since a single defective X allele is enough to express it in a male, whereas a female needs two.

CYSTIC FIBROSIS is an autosomal RECESSIVE disorder caused by mutation in the CFTR gene, which codes for a chloride-ion channel. Thick, sticky mucus clogs the lungs and blocks the ducts of the pancreas, causing repeated infections and poor digestion.

(b) CHROMOSOMAL DISORDERS

These are caused by an abnormal NUMBER of chromosomes (aneuploidy), usually arising from NON-DISJUNCTION - the failure of chromosomes to separate during meiosis, so a gamete carries one too many or one too few.

DOWN SYNDROME (TRISOMY 21) is caused by an EXTRA copy of chromosome 21, so the cells have 47 chromosomes instead of 46. Affected individuals show a characteristic facial appearance, short stature, a broad palm with a single crease, and some degree of mental retardation. The chance of a trisomy-21 child rises sharply with the mother's age.

TURNER SYNDROME affects females who have only ONE X chromosome (45, X0) instead of two. Such women are sterile, short in stature, and lack full sexual maturity, because the second sex chromosome is missing.

KLINEFELTER SYNDROME affects males who have an EXTRA X chromosome (47, XXY). They are usually tall, sterile, and show some feminine features such as breast development (gynaecomastia), because of the additional X.

24.3 PEDIGREE ANALYSIS

A PEDIGREE is a family tree that records a trait across several generations using standard symbols - squares for males, circles for females, filled symbols for affected individuals, and horizontal lines for matings. By studying a pedigree a geneticist can work out whether a trait is DOMINANT or RECESSIVE and whether it is AUTOSOMAL or SEX-LINKED, and can estimate the risk that future children will be affected. For example, a recessive trait may skip generations and appear in children of unaffected (carrier) parents, whereas an X-linked recessive trait appears mainly in males and passes from carrier mothers to sons. Pedigree analysis is a key tool in genetic counselling.

24.4 GENETIC COUNSELLING AND PRENATAL DIAGNOSIS

GENETIC COUNSELLING is guidance given to families about the risk, diagnosis, management and prevention of genetic disorders. A counsellor studies the family history, draws a pedigree, may order tests, explains the risk to prospective parents in a clear and non-directive way, and helps them make informed decisions.

PRENATAL DIAGNOSIS means testing the unborn baby for genetic or chromosomal defects. The main techniques are:

AMNIOCENTESIS: a needle is used to withdraw a small sample of the AMNIOTIC FLUID surrounding the foetus (usually around the 14th-16th week). Foetal cells in the fluid are cultured and their chromosomes examined (karyotyping), and biochemical tests are done. It can detect Down syndrome, sex of the foetus, and many metabolic and chromosomal disorders.

CHORIONIC VILLUS SAMPLING (CVS): a sample of the placental tissue (chorionic villi) is taken earlier in pregnancy for similar analysis.

Other aids include ULTRASOUND scanning and blood tests. Prenatal diagnosis lets a family prepare for or, where the law allows, decide about a seriously affected pregnancy.

MISUSE OF AMNIOCENTESIS: because amniocentesis reveals the SEX of the foetus, it has been badly MISUSED for sex determination leading to female foeticide. This has distorted the sex ratio in some regions. For this reason India has LEGALLY BANNED the use of amniocentesis and other techniques for sex determination under the PC-PNDT Act; the tests are permitted only to detect genetic and chromosomal disorders, not to select the sex of the child.

24.5 EUGENICS, EUPHENICS AND EUTHENICS

EUGENICS is the idea of "improving" the human race by controlling breeding - encouraging reproduction among people with supposedly desirable traits (positive eugenics) or discouraging it among those with undesirable traits (negative eugenics). Historically eugenics was misused to justify forced sterilisation and racism, and it is now regarded as ethically unacceptable. EUPHENICS is the treatment of a genetic defect AFTER birth by medical or dietary means (for example, the special diet for PKU or insulin for diabetes) - it improves the phenotype without changing the genes. EUTHENICS is the improvement of human welfare by bettering the ENVIRONMENT - nutrition, education, sanitation and living conditions - rather than the genes.

24.6 THE HUMAN GENOME PROJECT

The HUMAN GENOME PROJECT (HGP) was a giant international collaboration begun in 1990 and essentially completed in 2003. Its GOALS were to identify all the genes in human DNA (about 20,000-25,000), to determine the SEQUENCE of the roughly 3 BILLION base pairs that make up the human genome, to store this information in databases, and to consider the ethical, legal and social issues arising from it.

FINDINGS: the human genome contains far fewer genes than expected; less than 2% of the DNA actually codes for proteins, while much of the rest is non-coding (once loosely called "junk" DNA). Any two humans are more than 99.9% identical in their DNA. Chromosome 1 has the most genes and the Y chromosome the fewest.

APPLICATIONS: the HGP is transforming medicine - it helps identify disease genes, design better diagnostics, develop gene therapy and personalised ("pharmacogenomic") medicine, and understand human evolution and diversity. Its data are freely available to researchers worldwide.

24.7 DNA FINGERPRINTING

DNA FINGERPRINTING (DNA profiling), developed by Alec Jeffreys, is a technique for identifying individuals from their DNA. Its PRINCIPLE rests on the fact that certain regions of the genome contain short base sequences REPEATED many times in tandem - VARIABLE NUMBER TANDEM REPEATS (VNTRs), also called minisatellites. The NUMBER of repeats at these sites differs from person to person, so the pattern of fragment lengths is essentially UNIQUE to each individual (except identical twins). In the classic method DNA is cut with restriction enzymes, the fragments are separated by gel electrophoresis according to size, transferred to a membrane (Southern blotting) and revealed with labelled probes, giving a pattern of bands like a supermarket bar code. Because a child inherits half of these repeats from each parent, the bands can be matched to parents.

APPLICATIONS: DNA fingerprinting is used in FORENSIC science to link a suspect to blood, hair or semen left at a crime scene; in PATERNITY and maternity disputes to establish biological parentage; in identifying victims of disasters; and in settling questions of pedigree and immigration. Only a tiny sample of DNA is needed, and it can be amplified by the polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

24.8 GENETICALLY MODIFIED ORGANISMS AND ETHICAL ISSUES

A GENETICALLY MODIFIED ORGANISM (GMO) is one whose genome has been deliberately altered by inserting a foreign gene using recombinant-DNA (genetic engineering) technology. Examples include Bt cotton and Bt brinjal (carrying a bacterial gene that resists insect pests), Golden Rice (enriched with pro-vitamin A), and bacteria engineered to make human insulin. GMOs promise higher yields, pest resistance and better nutrition, but they raise ETHICAL AND SOCIAL concerns: possible effects on human health and allergies, escape of engineered genes into wild species, loss of biodiversity, and the control of seeds by large companies. Many countries therefore regulate GMOs strictly through biosafety committees.

24.9 PLANT AND ANIMAL BREEDING

Long before genetic engineering, humans improved crops and livestock by conventional BREEDING.

SELECTIVE BREEDING (ARTIFICIAL SELECTION): choosing and breeding only those plants or animals that show desired qualities - higher yield, more milk, disease resistance - generation after generation.

HYBRIDIZATION: crossing two genetically different parents (varieties, or even species) to combine their good traits in the offspring. The offspring often show HYBRID VIGOUR (heterosis) - being healthier and more productive than either parent.

MUTATION BREEDING: deliberately inducing mutations with radiation or chemicals and then selecting useful new variants (for example, disease-resistant or dwarf varieties).

THE GREEN REVOLUTION of the 1960s-70s dramatically raised food-grain production in India and elsewhere by combining HIGH-YIELDING dwarf varieties of wheat and rice (developed by breeders such as Norman Borlaug and, in India, M. S. Swaminathan) with irrigation, fertilisers and pesticides. It made the country self-sufficient in food grains, though it also brought concerns about soil and water.

BIOFORTIFICATION is the breeding of crops with HIGHER levels of vitamins, minerals or proteins to improve public nutrition - for example, iron-rich and protein-rich cereals, vitamin-A-enriched carrots and Golden Rice.

24.10 BIOPIRACY AND BIOETHICS

BIOPIRACY is the exploitation of the biological resources and traditional knowledge of a country or community by others (often companies from other nations) WITHOUT proper authorisation or fair sharing of benefits - for example, patenting products based on neem, turmeric or basmati rice. Nations now protect their resources through laws and international agreements.

BIOETHICS is the study of the moral questions raised by advances in biology and medicine. It asks how far we should go in manipulating life - in cloning, genetic engineering, prenatal selection and the use of genetic information - and insists on consent, fairness, safety and respect for life. Genetics has given society great power; bioethics reminds us to use it wisely.

SUMMARY

- Genetic disorders are of two kinds: MENDELIAN (single-gene) and CHROMOSOMAL (whole-chromosome).
- Autosomal recessive single-gene disorders include sickle-cell anaemia (defective HbS haemoglobin), thalassaemia (too little haemoglobin), phenylketonuria (enzyme defect) and cystic fibrosis; sex-linked recessive disorders include haemophilia and red-green colour blindness, both commoner in males.
- Chromosomal disorders arise from non-disjunction: Down syndrome (trisomy 21, 47 chromosomes), Turner syndrome (45, X0 females) and Klinefelter syndrome (47, XXY males).
- A pedigree (family tree) reveals whether a trait is dominant/recessive and autosomal/sex-linked and helps estimate risk.
- Genetic counselling advises families about genetic risk; prenatal diagnosis (amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling, ultrasound) detects defects before birth. Amniocentesis has been misused for sex determination and is legally banned for that purpose in India.
- Eugenics (controlling breeding - now unacceptable), euphenics (treating a defect after birth) and euthenics (improving the environment) are distinct approaches.
- The Human Genome Project (1990-2003) sequenced the ~3 billion base pairs and ~20,000-25,000 genes of human DNA, revealing that humans are >99.9% alike and that <2% of DNA codes for protein.
- DNA fingerprinting relies on variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs) whose pattern is unique to each individual; it is used in forensics, paternity testing and identification.
- Crop and livestock improvement uses selective breeding, hybridization (giving hybrid vigour) and mutation breeding; the Green Revolution and biofortification improved food supply and nutrition.
- GMOs offer benefits but raise ethical concerns; biopiracy and bioethics remind us to use genetic power responsibly.

topics.name: Chromosomal Disorders
topics.description: Disorders caused by an abnormal number of chromosomes arising from non-disjunction: Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Turner syndrome (45, X0) and Klinefelter syndrome (47, XXY).

topics.description: Pedigree analysis, genetic counselling, and prenatal diagnostic techniques (amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling, ultrasound), including the misuse of amniocentesis for sex determination and its legal ban.

topics.name: The Human Genome Project
topics.description: The Human Genome Project: its goals, key findings (number of genes and base pairs, >99.9% similarity, non-coding DNA) and its applications in medicine and biology.

topics.description: DNA fingerprinting: its principle based on variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs) and its forensic, paternity and identification applications.

An autosomal recessive metabolic disorder in which phenylalanine cannot be converted to tyrosine, harming the brain if untreated.
An X-linked recessive disorder in which blood fails to clot due to a missing clotting factor; commoner in males.
An X-linked recessive defect of the cone pigments causing inability to distinguish red from green; commoner in males.
The failure of chromosomes to separate during meiosis, producing gametes with an abnormal chromosome number.

A chromosomal disorder in females having a single X chromosome (45, X0), who are sterile and short-statured.
A chromosomal disorder in males having an extra X chromosome (47, XXY), who are tall and sterile.
A prenatal test in which amniotic fluid is sampled and foetal cells examined for chromosomal and metabolic disorders.
The international project (1990-2003) that sequenced the ~3 billion base pairs and mapped the genes of human DNA.

The crossing of two genetically different parents to combine desired traits, often producing vigorous hybrid offspring.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Genetics and Society (NIOS Senior Secondary Biology)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Answer briefly for short-answer questions and give full explanations for long-answer questions. Use correct genetic terms.

questions.question: Distinguish between a Mendelian genetic disorder and a chromosomal disorder, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: A Mendelian (single-gene) disorder is caused by mutation in a single gene and is inherited according to Mendel's rules; example - sickle-cell anaemia. A chromosomal disorder is caused by a change in the number or structure of whole chromosomes, usually from non-disjunction; example - Down syndrome (trisomy 21).
questions.explanation: Single-gene vs whole-chromosome cause, with examples.

questions.question: Explain the genetic basis of sickle-cell anaemia and why carriers are common in malaria-prone regions.
questions.answer: Sickle-cell anaemia is autosomal recessive. A single base change in the beta-globin gene substitutes valine for glutamic acid, producing abnormal haemoglobin (HbS). At low oxygen the red cells become rigid and sickle-shaped, block vessels and are destroyed, causing anaemia. A person with two mutant alleles is affected; one mutant allele makes a healthy carrier. Carriers are partly protected against malaria, so the allele persists in malaria-prone regions.
questions.explanation: Base change -> HbS -> sickling; heterozygote advantage against malaria.

questions.question: Why are X-linked recessive disorders such as haemophilia and colour blindness more common in males than in females?
questions.answer: The genes for these disorders lie on the X chromosome. A male has only one X, so a single defective allele is enough to express the disorder. A female has two X chromosomes, so she must inherit two defective alleles to be affected; with one she is only a carrier. Therefore these disorders appear far more often in males.
questions.explanation: One X in males means a single recessive allele is expressed.

questions.question: What is non-disjunction and how does it lead to Down syndrome?
questions.answer: Non-disjunction is the failure of chromosomes to separate during meiosis, so a gamete receives one chromosome too many or too few. If a gamete carrying an extra chromosome 21 fuses with a normal gamete, the child has three copies of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21, 47 chromosomes in all) - this is Down syndrome, marked by characteristic features and mental retardation.

questions.question: Compare Turner syndrome and Klinefelter syndrome.
questions.answer: Turner syndrome affects females with a single X chromosome (45, X0); they are sterile, short-statured and lack full sexual maturity. Klinefelter syndrome affects males with an extra X chromosome (47, XXY); they are tall, sterile and may show feminine features such as breast development. Both result from non-disjunction of the sex chromosomes.

questions.question: What is amniocentesis? Why has its use for sex determination been banned in India?
questions.answer: Amniocentesis is a prenatal test in which a sample of amniotic fluid surrounding the foetus is withdrawn and the foetal cells are examined for chromosomal and metabolic disorders. Because it also reveals the sex of the foetus, it was misused for sex determination leading to female foeticide and a distorted sex ratio. India has therefore legally banned its use for sex determination, allowing it only for detecting genetic and chromosomal disorders.
questions.explanation: Fluid sampling for karyotyping; banned for sex selection to stop female foeticide.

questions.question: State the main goals of the Human Genome Project.
questions.answer: The main goals of the Human Genome Project were: to identify all the genes in human DNA (about 20,000-25,000); to determine the sequence of the roughly 3 billion base pairs of the human genome; to store the information in databases and make it available; and to consider the ethical, legal and social issues arising from the knowledge.
questions.explanation: Identify genes, sequence base pairs, store data, address ELSI.

questions.question: State the principle of DNA fingerprinting and give two applications.
questions.answer: DNA fingerprinting is based on variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs) - short sequences repeated a different number of times at certain sites in each person's DNA, so the pattern of fragment lengths is unique to each individual (except identical twins). Applications: forensic identification of a suspect from blood or hair at a crime scene, and paternity testing to establish biological parentage.
questions.explanation: VNTRs give a unique banding pattern; used in forensics and paternity tests.

questions.question: Describe the methods used to improve crops and livestock: selective breeding, hybridization and mutation breeding. Mention the Green Revolution and biofortification.
questions.answer: Selective breeding (artificial selection) means choosing and breeding only those plants or animals with desired qualities - higher yield, more milk, disease resistance - generation after generation. Hybridization means crossing two genetically different parents to combine their good traits; the offspring often show hybrid vigour (heterosis), being healthier and more productive than either parent. Mutation breeding means deliberately inducing mutations with radiation or chemicals and selecting useful new variants, such as disease-resistant or dwarf varieties. The Green Revolution of the 1960s-70s combined high-yielding dwarf varieties of wheat and rice with irrigation, fertilisers and pesticides, making India self-sufficient in food grains. Biofortification breeds crops with higher levels of vitamins, minerals or proteins - for example iron-rich cereals and vitamin-A-enriched Golden Rice - to improve public nutrition.
questions.explanation: Three breeding methods plus Green Revolution and biofortification.

questions.question: Discuss the ethical and social issues raised by genetically modified organisms and by biopiracy. What does bioethics contribute?
questions.answer: A genetically modified organism (GMO) has a foreign gene inserted by genetic engineering - for example Bt cotton, Golden Rice or insulin-making bacteria. GMOs promise higher yields, pest resistance and better nutrition, but raise concerns: possible effects on human health and allergies, escape of engineered genes into wild species, loss of biodiversity, and the control of seeds by large companies. Biopiracy is the unauthorised exploitation of a country's biological resources or traditional knowledge without fair benefit-sharing - for example patents based on neem, turmeric or basmati. Bioethics is the study of the moral questions raised by such advances; it asks how far we should manipulate life and insists on consent, fairness, safety and respect for life, guiding society to use genetic power responsibly.
questions.explanation: GMO risks, biopiracy definition, and the guiding role of bioethics.

questions.question: The abnormal haemoglobin in sickle-cell anaemia is denoted ____.
In phenylketonuria the amino acid ____ accumulates and harms the brain.
questions.explanation: The enzyme converting it to tyrosine is missing.

questions.question: Cystic fibrosis is caused by mutation in the ____ gene coding a chloride channel.
questions.explanation: CFTR = cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator.

questions.question: Haemophilia is a sex-linked recessive disorder carried on the ____ chromosome.
A woman with one defective colour-blindness allele is a healthy ____.
questions.explanation: She needs two alleles to be affected.

questions.question: The failure of chromosomes to separate during meiosis is called ____.
Down syndrome is also called trisomy ____.
Klinefelter syndrome has the chromosome constitution 47, ____.
questions.explanation: An extra X in a male.

questions.question: A ____ is a family tree used to trace the inheritance of a trait.
In ____ a sample of amniotic fluid is withdrawn to test the foetus.
The human genome consists of about 3 ____ base pairs.
Any two humans are more than ____ percent identical in their DNA.
DNA fingerprinting is based on repeated sequences called ____.
The extra vigour of hybrid offspring is called hybrid ____ or heterosis.
The unauthorised exploitation of a country's bioresources is called ____.
Name any four single-gene (Mendelian) human disorders.
questions.answer: Four Mendelian disorders are sickle-cell anaemia, thalassaemia, phenylketonuria and haemophilia (others include colour blindness and cystic fibrosis).

questions.question: Explain why sickle-cell anaemia is called a qualitative defect while thalassaemia is a quantitative defect.
questions.answer: In sickle-cell anaemia a base change produces a structurally abnormal haemoglobin (HbS) - the haemoglobin is of the wrong quality, so it is a qualitative defect. In thalassaemia the globin chains are structurally normal but too few are made, so there is too little haemoglobin - a quantitative defect.
questions.explanation: Wrong haemoglobin vs too little haemoglobin.

questions.question: How is phenylketonuria managed?
questions.answer: PKU is detected by newborn screening and managed with a phenylalanine-restricted diet so that the amino acid does not accumulate and damage the brain.
questions.explanation: Early detection plus a low-phenylalanine diet.

questions.question: What causes the symptoms of cystic fibrosis?
questions.answer: Mutation in the CFTR gene disrupts a chloride-ion channel, so thick sticky mucus forms. It clogs the lungs, causing repeated infections, and blocks the pancreatic ducts, impairing digestion.

questions.question: Using genetics, explain why a colour-blind daughter is rarer than a colour-blind son.
questions.answer: The colour-blindness allele is X-linked recessive. A son has only one X, so a single defective allele (inherited from a carrier mother) makes him colour blind. A daughter has two X chromosomes and needs the defective allele on both - one from a carrier or colour-blind mother and one from a colour-blind father - which is much less likely. Hence colour-blind daughters are rarer.
questions.explanation: Daughters need two defective X alleles; sons only one.

questions.question: A carrier mother and a normal father have children. What is the chance that a son is haemophilic?
questions.answer: The mother carries one normal and one defective X; the father gives a normal X to daughters and a Y to sons. Each son has a 1/2 chance of receiving the defective X, so the chance that a son is haemophilic is 1/2 (50%).
questions.explanation: Half the sons inherit the affected X.

questions.question: Explain the pattern of inheritance seen in the haemophilia pedigree of Queen Victoria's family.
questions.answer: Haemophilia is X-linked recessive. Queen Victoria was a carrier and passed the defective X to some children. Carrier daughters (unaffected) transmitted it into other royal families, while affected sons showed the bleeding disorder. Thus the trait passed mainly through carrier females to affected males - the criss-cross pattern typical of X-linked recessive inheritance.
questions.explanation: Carrier females transmit to affected males across generations.

questions.question: List the chromosome numbers in Down, Turner and Klinefelter syndromes.
questions.answer: Down syndrome: 47 chromosomes (trisomy 21). Turner syndrome: 45 chromosomes (45, X0). Klinefelter syndrome: 47 chromosomes (47, XXY).

questions.question: Describe the main features of Down syndrome.
questions.answer: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) shows a characteristic facial appearance, short stature, a broad palm with a single crease, and some degree of mental retardation. It results from an extra chromosome 21, and its frequency rises with the mother's age.
questions.explanation: Facial features, single palm crease, short stature, mental retardation.

questions.question: Why are individuals with Turner and Klinefelter syndromes usually sterile?
questions.answer: In both, the sex-chromosome constitution is abnormal (45, X0 in Turner and 47, XXY in Klinefelter) so the gonads do not develop or function normally, and normal gametes are not produced. Hence they are sterile.

questions.question: What symbols are used in a pedigree for males, females and affected individuals?
questions.answer: In a pedigree a square represents a male, a circle represents a female, and a filled (shaded) symbol represents an affected individual. A horizontal line joining a square and a circle shows a mating.
questions.explanation: Square = male, circle = female, shaded = affected.

questions.question: Two unaffected parents have a child with an autosomal recessive disorder. Explain how this is possible and give the risk for the next child.
questions.answer: Both parents must be heterozygous carriers (Aa). Each carries one normal and one recessive allele but is unaffected. When both pass the recessive allele the child is aa and affected. From an Aa x Aa cross, each child has a 1/4 (25%) chance of being affected, so the risk for the next child is 1 in 4.

questions.question: What is the role of a genetic counsellor?
questions.answer: A genetic counsellor studies the family history and draws a pedigree, may arrange tests, explains the risk of a genetic disorder to prospective parents in a clear, non-directive way, and helps them make informed decisions about having children or managing a disorder.
questions.explanation: Assess risk, inform, and support family decisions.

questions.question: Why was a law needed to regulate the use of amniocentesis in India?
questions.answer: Because amniocentesis reveals the sex of the foetus, it was misused for sex determination, leading to female foeticide and a distorted sex ratio in some regions. A law (the PC-PNDT Act) was needed to ban its use for sex determination while still allowing it to detect genuine genetic and chromosomal disorders, so that a useful medical test is not abused.
questions.explanation: To stop female foeticide while keeping the medical use.

questions.question: State two important findings of the Human Genome Project.
questions.answer: Two findings: the human genome has only about 20,000-25,000 genes, far fewer than expected; and any two humans are more than 99.9% identical in their DNA, with less than 2% of the DNA coding for protein.

questions.question: How is the Human Genome Project useful to medicine?
questions.answer: By revealing the sequence and location of genes, the project helps identify disease genes, design better diagnostic tests, develop gene therapy, and create personalised (pharmacogenomic) medicine tailored to a patient's genetic make-up. It also deepens understanding of human evolution and diversity.
questions.explanation: Disease-gene identification, diagnostics, gene therapy, personalised medicine.

questions.question: What is meant by non-coding DNA?
questions.answer: Non-coding DNA is the large part of the genome (more than 98% in humans) that does not code for proteins. It was once loosely called 'junk' DNA, but much of it has regulatory and structural roles.
questions.explanation: DNA that does not code for protein; formerly called junk DNA.

questions.question: Outline the main steps in preparing a DNA fingerprint.
questions.answer: The DNA is extracted and cut into fragments with restriction enzymes. The fragments are separated by gel electrophoresis according to size, transferred to a membrane (Southern blotting), and the VNTR regions are revealed with labelled probes, giving a pattern of bands like a bar code. Tiny samples can first be amplified by PCR.
questions.explanation: Cut -> separate by electrophoresis -> blot -> probe -> band pattern.

questions.question: How can DNA fingerprinting settle a paternity dispute?
questions.answer: Each child inherits half of its VNTR bands from each biological parent. In a paternity test the child's DNA fingerprint is compared with the mother's and the alleged father's. Every band in the child must be present in either the mother or the true father; if bands unmatched by the mother are also absent in the man, he is excluded, whereas a full match supports paternity.
questions.explanation: Child's bands must come from each true parent.

questions.question: Distinguish between hybridization and mutation breeding.
questions.answer: Hybridization crosses two genetically different parents to combine their desirable traits, often producing vigorous hybrid offspring (heterosis). Mutation breeding deliberately induces mutations using radiation or chemicals and then selects useful new variants, such as disease-resistant or dwarf types. Hybridization recombines existing variation; mutation breeding creates new variation.
questions.explanation: Crossing parents vs inducing new mutations.

questions.question: What is biofortification and why is it useful?
questions.answer: Biofortification is the breeding of crops with higher levels of vitamins, minerals or proteins - for example iron-rich cereals and vitamin-A-enriched Golden Rice. It is useful because it improves public nutrition and helps combat deficiency diseases through everyday food.

questions.question: Give three concerns raised by the use of genetically modified organisms.
questions.answer: Concerns about GMOs include: possible effects on human health such as allergies; the escape of engineered genes into wild species and loss of biodiversity; and the control of seeds and agriculture by a few large companies. These are why GMOs are regulated by biosafety committees.
questions.explanation: Health risks, gene escape/biodiversity loss, corporate seed control.

questions.question: Describe sickle-cell anaemia and thalassaemia and compare them.
questions.answer: Sickle-cell anaemia is an autosomal recessive disorder. A single base change in the beta-globin gene replaces glutamic acid with valine, producing abnormal haemoglobin HbS. At low oxygen the red cells become rigid and sickle-shaped, block small vessels and are destroyed rapidly, causing anaemia and pain. Two mutant alleles (HbS HbS) give the disease; one mutant allele gives a healthy carrier with sickle-cell trait, who is partly protected against malaria. Thalassaemia is also autosomal recessive but here one of the globin chains (alpha or beta) is made in reduced amount or not at all, so too little normal haemoglobin is produced; patients have chronic anaemia and often need repeated blood transfusions. Comparison: sickle-cell anaemia is a QUALITATIVE defect (structurally abnormal haemoglobin), whereas thalassaemia is a QUANTITATIVE defect (too little haemoglobin). Both are recessive blood disorders inherited in a Mendelian manner.
questions.explanation: HbS structural defect vs reduced globin synthesis; both recessive.

questions.question: Explain sex-linked inheritance using haemophilia as an example, and analyse the expected offspring of a carrier woman married to a normal man.
questions.answer: Sex-linked (X-linked) inheritance concerns genes on the X chromosome. Haemophilia is X-linked recessive: the allele lies on the X, and because a male has only one X (XY), a single defective allele makes him haemophilic, while a female (XX) needs two defective alleles to be affected and with one is only a carrier. Consider a carrier woman (X^H X^h) married to a normal man (X^H Y). The daughters receive one X from each parent: half are normal (X^H X^H) and half are carriers (X^H X^h) - none are affected. The sons receive their single X from the mother and Y from the father: half receive X^H (normal) and half X^h (haemophilic). So among the children we expect normal daughters and carrier daughters in equal numbers, and normal sons and affected sons in equal numbers - that is, half the sons are likely to be haemophilic while no daughter is affected. This explains why haemophilia appears mainly in males and passes through carrier mothers.
questions.explanation: X-linked recessive cross: carrier mother x normal father -> half sons affected, daughters carriers/normal.

questions.question: What are chromosomal disorders? Describe Down, Turner and Klinefelter syndromes.
questions.answer: Chromosomal disorders are caused by an abnormal number (or structure) of chromosomes, usually arising from non-disjunction - the failure of chromosomes to separate during meiosis, so a gamete carries one chromosome too many or too few. Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is caused by an extra chromosome 21, giving 47 chromosomes; affected people show a characteristic facial appearance, short stature, a single palm crease and mental retardation, and the risk rises with maternal age. Turner syndrome affects females with a single X chromosome (45, X0); they are sterile, short-statured and lack full sexual maturity. Klinefelter syndrome affects males with an extra X chromosome (47, XXY); they are usually tall, sterile and show some feminine features such as breast development. All three arise from non-disjunction, of chromosome 21 in Down syndrome and of the sex chromosomes in Turner and Klinefelter syndromes.
questions.explanation: Non-disjunction -> aneuploidy; three named syndromes described.

questions.question: Explain genetic counselling and prenatal diagnosis, and discuss the misuse of amniocentesis.
questions.answer: Genetic counselling is guidance given to families about the risk, diagnosis, management and prevention of genetic disorders. A counsellor studies the family history, draws a pedigree, may order tests, explains the risk to prospective parents in a clear and non-directive way, and helps them make informed decisions. Prenatal diagnosis tests the unborn baby for defects. In amniocentesis a small sample of amniotic fluid is withdrawn (around the 14th-16th week); foetal cells are cultured and their chromosomes examined by karyotyping, and biochemical tests are done, so that Down syndrome and many metabolic and chromosomal disorders can be detected. Chorionic villus sampling and ultrasound give further information. Misuse: because amniocentesis also reveals the sex of the foetus, it has been badly misused for sex determination, leading to female foeticide and a distorted sex ratio. India has therefore legally banned its use for sex determination (PC-PNDT Act), permitting it only to detect genetic and chromosomal disorders. Thus a valuable medical test must be used ethically.
questions.explanation: Counselling, amniocentesis/CVS, and the legal ban on sex determination.

questions.question: Describe the Human Genome Project - its goals, findings and applications.
questions.answer: The Human Genome Project (HGP) was a large international collaboration begun in 1990 and essentially completed in 2003. Its goals were to identify all the genes in human DNA (about 20,000-25,000), to determine the sequence of the roughly 3 billion base pairs of the genome, to store the information in accessible databases, and to consider the ethical, legal and social issues arising from it. Findings: the genome has far fewer genes than expected; less than 2% of the DNA codes for protein while most is non-coding; any two humans are more than 99.9% identical; chromosome 1 has the most genes and the Y chromosome the fewest. Applications: the project is transforming medicine by helping to identify disease genes, design better diagnostics, develop gene therapy and personalised (pharmacogenomic) medicine, and it deepens our understanding of human evolution and diversity. Its data are freely shared with researchers worldwide.
questions.explanation: Goals, key findings and medical applications of the HGP.

questions.question: Explain the principle of DNA fingerprinting and describe its applications.
questions.answer: DNA fingerprinting (DNA profiling), developed by Alec Jeffreys, identifies individuals from their DNA. Its principle rests on variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs) - short base sequences repeated many times in tandem at certain sites in the genome. The number of repeats at these sites differs from person to person, so the resulting pattern of fragment lengths is essentially unique to each individual (except identical twins). In the classic method the DNA is cut with restriction enzymes, the fragments are separated by gel electrophoresis according to size, transferred to a membrane by Southern blotting and revealed with labelled probes, giving a pattern of bands like a bar code; tiny samples can first be amplified by PCR. Because a child inherits half its repeats from each parent, the bands can be matched to parents. Applications: forensic science, linking a suspect to blood, hair or semen at a crime scene; paternity and maternity disputes; identification of victims of disasters; and questions of pedigree and immigration.
questions.explanation: VNTR principle plus forensic, paternity and identification uses.

questions.question: Describe the methods of crop and livestock improvement and explain the Green Revolution.
questions.answer: Humans improve crops and livestock mainly by conventional breeding. Selective breeding (artificial selection) chooses and breeds only those plants or animals with desired qualities - higher yield, more milk, disease resistance - generation after generation. Hybridization crosses two genetically different parents to combine their good traits; the offspring often show hybrid vigour (heterosis), being healthier and more productive than either parent. Mutation breeding deliberately induces mutations with radiation or chemicals and selects useful new variants such as disease-resistant or dwarf types. The Green Revolution of the 1960s-70s combined high-yielding dwarf varieties of wheat and rice (developed by breeders such as Norman Borlaug and, in India, M. S. Swaminathan) with irrigation, fertilisers and pesticides, greatly raising food-grain production and making India self-sufficient in food grains, though it also raised concerns about soil and water. Biofortification further breeds crops richer in vitamins, minerals and proteins to improve nutrition.
questions.explanation: Selective breeding, hybridization, mutation breeding, Green Revolution, biofortification.

questions.question: Evaluate the ethical and social issues raised by modern genetics, including GMOs, eugenics, biopiracy and bioethics.
questions.answer: Modern genetics gives society great power, and with it responsibilities. Genetically modified organisms (GMOs) carry a foreign gene inserted by genetic engineering - such as Bt cotton, Golden Rice or insulin-making bacteria - and promise higher yields, pest resistance and better nutrition; but they raise concerns about human health and allergies, escape of engineered genes into wild species, loss of biodiversity, and control of seeds by large companies, so they are regulated by biosafety committees. Eugenics, the attempt to 'improve' humanity by controlling breeding, was historically misused to justify forced sterilisation and racism and is now regarded as ethically unacceptable; euphenics (treating a defect after birth) and euthenics (improving the environment) are acceptable alternatives. Biopiracy is the unauthorised exploitation of a nation's biological resources or traditional knowledge without fair benefit-sharing, as in patents based on neem or turmeric, and nations now guard against it. Bioethics is the study of the moral questions raised by these advances; it insists on consent, fairness, safety and respect for life, reminding us to use genetic power wisely.
questions.explanation: Balances GMO benefits/risks, rejects eugenics, defines biopiracy, and stresses bioethics.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A couple who are both healthy already have one child affected by sickle-cell anaemia. On testing, both parents are found to carry one HbS allele.

(a) What are the genotypes of the two parents?
(b) Why are the parents themselves healthy?
(c) What is the chance that their next child will be affected?
(d) Why does the HbS allele remain common in some regions?
questions.answer: (a) Both parents are heterozygous carriers, genotype HbA HbS. (b) Each has one normal allele (HbA) which makes enough normal haemoglobin, so they are healthy carriers showing only sickle-cell trait. (c) From HbA HbS x HbA HbS, one quarter of the children are HbS HbS, so the chance the next child is affected is 1/4 (25%). (d) Carriers are partly protected against malaria, so the allele persists in malaria-prone regions (heterozygote advantage).
questions.explanation: Carrier x carrier; 1/4 affected; malaria protection keeps the allele common.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A woman whose father was colour blind marries a man with normal colour vision. Colour blindness is X-linked recessive.

(a) What is the woman's genotype for the colour-vision gene?
(b) Can any of their daughters be colour blind?
(c) What fraction of their sons is expected to be colour blind?
(d) From whom did the woman inherit the defective allele?
questions.answer: (a) Her father was colour blind (X^c Y) and gave her his X^c, so she is a carrier, X^C X^c. (b) The father has normal vision (X^C Y) and gives daughters X^C, so no daughter receives two defective alleles - none of the daughters can be colour blind (they may be carriers). (c) Sons get their X from the carrier mother, so half of the sons are expected to be colour blind (1/2). (d) She inherited the defective X^c allele from her colour-blind father.
questions.explanation: Carrier mother x normal father; daughters not affected, half of sons affected; allele from father.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A newborn is found to have 47 chromosomes, with three copies of chromosome 21. The baby shows a characteristic facial appearance and a single palm crease.

(a) Name the disorder.
(b) What is the underlying error in cell division that causes it?
(c) State two clinical features.
(d) Which parental factor increases its risk?
questions.answer: (a) The disorder is Down syndrome (trisomy 21). (b) It is caused by non-disjunction - the failure of chromosome 21 to separate during meiosis - so a gamete carries an extra chromosome 21. (c) Two features: a characteristic facial appearance and a single palm crease (also short stature and mental retardation). (d) The risk increases with the mother's (advanced maternal) age.
questions.explanation: Trisomy 21 from non-disjunction; features; risk rises with maternal age.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Two patients are examined. Patient P is a short, sterile female whose cells have 45 chromosomes (one X only). Patient Q is a tall, sterile male whose cells have 47 chromosomes (XXY).

(a) Name the syndrome in P.
(b) Name the syndrome in Q.
(c) What common type of error produced both conditions?
(d) Why are both patients sterile?
questions.answer: (a) Patient P has Turner syndrome (45, X0). (b) Patient Q has Klinefelter syndrome (47, XXY). (c) Both were produced by non-disjunction of the sex chromosomes during meiosis. (d) In both, the abnormal sex-chromosome constitution means the gonads do not develop or function normally, so normal gametes are not formed and the patients are sterile.
questions.explanation: Turner (X0) and Klinefelter (XXY); both from sex-chromosome non-disjunction; sterile.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A 40-year-old pregnant woman is advised to undergo prenatal testing because of her age. A sample of the fluid around the foetus is taken and the foetal cells are karyotyped.

(a) Name the prenatal test described.
(b) Which fluid is sampled?
(c) Name one disorder it can detect.
(d) For what purpose is this test banned in India?
questions.answer: (a) The test is amniocentesis. (b) The amniotic fluid surrounding the foetus is sampled. (c) It can detect Down syndrome (also other chromosomal and metabolic disorders). (d) Its use for sex determination is banned in India (to prevent female foeticide); it is allowed only for detecting genetic and chromosomal disorders.
questions.explanation: Amniocentesis; amniotic fluid; detects Down syndrome; banned for sex determination.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In a certain district the number of girls per 1000 boys has fallen sharply over two decades. Investigators link this to the misuse of a prenatal diagnostic technique.

(a) Which technique was most likely misused?
(b) What information did it provide that led to the misuse?
(c) What social practice caused the falling sex ratio?
(d) What legal step was taken to prevent this?
questions.answer: (a) Amniocentesis (a prenatal diagnostic technique) was most likely misused. (b) It revealed the sex of the foetus. (c) This information was used for sex-selective abortion (female foeticide), lowering the number of girls. (d) A law (the PC-PNDT Act) was passed banning the use of amniocentesis and similar techniques for sex determination, allowing them only to detect genetic and chromosomal disorders.
questions.explanation: Amniocentesis reveals sex -> female foeticide -> banned by PC-PNDT Act.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

An international project that ran from 1990 to 2003 aimed to read the entire genetic instruction book of human beings and made its data freely available.

(a) Name the project.
(b) About how many base pairs did it sequence?
(c) About how many genes were found?
(d) State one medical application of its results.
questions.answer: (a) The project is the Human Genome Project. (b) It sequenced about 3 billion base pairs. (c) About 20,000-25,000 genes were found. (d) One medical application: identifying disease genes and developing personalised medicine and gene therapy (also better diagnostic tests).
questions.explanation: Human Genome Project; ~3 billion base pairs; ~20000-25000 genes; personalised medicine.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

At a crime scene, bloodstains are found. Forensic scientists prepare a DNA profile from the blood and compare it with profiles of three suspects.

(a) On what repeated sequences is the DNA profile based?
(b) By what technique are the DNA fragments separated?
(c) Why can the blood be matched to just one person?
(d) Name one other application of this technique.
questions.answer: (a) The profile is based on variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs). (b) The DNA fragments are separated by gel electrophoresis according to size. (c) Because the number of repeats at the VNTR sites differs between people, each person's banding pattern is essentially unique (except identical twins), so the blood matches only one person. (d) Another application: paternity testing (or identifying disaster victims).
questions.explanation: VNTRs; gel electrophoresis; unique pattern; paternity testing.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In the 1960s and 1970s India adopted new dwarf, high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice together with irrigation, fertilisers and pesticides, and grain production rose sharply.

(a) What is this period of change called?
(b) Name the two main cereal crops involved.
(c) What breeding method combines traits of two different parent varieties?
(d) What is the breeding of nutrient-rich crops called?
questions.answer: (a) It is called the Green Revolution. (b) The two main cereals were wheat and rice. (c) Hybridization combines the traits of two genetically different parent varieties (often giving hybrid vigour). (d) The breeding of crops richer in vitamins, minerals or proteins is called biofortification.
questions.explanation: Green Revolution; wheat and rice; hybridization; biofortification.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A company introduces an insect-resistant Bt crop carrying a bacterial gene, and later patents a product based on a plant traditionally used by local farmers without sharing benefits with them.

(a) What is the Bt crop an example of?
(b) State one ethical concern about such crops.
(c) What is the unauthorised patenting of traditional bioresources called?
(d) Which field studies such moral questions in biology?
questions.answer: (a) The Bt crop is an example of a genetically modified organism (GMO). (b) One ethical concern: possible harm to human health or the escape of the inserted gene into wild species and loss of biodiversity (or corporate control of seeds). (c) The unauthorised patenting of traditional bioresources and knowledge is called biopiracy. (d) The field that studies such moral questions in biology is bioethics.
